sections.title: "To bind what is written into the community"
sections.content: In the middle decades of the twentieth century, six Australian women authors wrote letters to each other, sustaining literary friendships over long distances and producing a rich record of the challenges of establishing and maintaining a career as a writer in this period. Literary historian and editor Carole Ferrier gathered these letters — 290 in total, covering the period from 1930 to 1957 — from a number of archives, including the National Library of Australia, the Mitchell Library, the State Library of Victoria and James Cook University Library, and published them under the title As Good As a Yarn With You: Letters Between Miles Franklin, Katharine Susannah Prichard, Jean Devanny, Marjorie Barnard, Flora Eldershaw and Eleanor Dark (Cambridge UP, 1992). Visualising the metadata from these letters offers alternative ways into the relationships between the people, places, dates and other information recorded within them, and potentially opens up fresh perspectives on this period of Australian literary history.

sections.title: Correspondence as a sustaining structure
sections.content: Excluded from the almost entirely male, university-centred circles in which Australian literary criticism was largely discussed, the women's correspondence serves as a place for them to both discuss their own writing and air ideas about literary criticism, as seen in this wartime letter from Marjorie Barnard to Eleanor Dark. "The next novel is taking root, or rather, the root having been there for a long time is beginning to put a shoot above ground — & all in a crazy mess of work and over work. About literary criticism — I feel it is necessary, but not as a direction to readers — reading is as private as writing. Nor, most certainly, as reward or punishment to writers. But simple as social affirmation or denial. ... If, as it is, all writing is communication, then it must be a two way traffic. Some sort of act of evaluation, a response other than the dispersed, haphazard one of buying and reading the book is necessary to complete the social circuit. To bind what is written into the community" (26 June 1944).

sections.title: Geographic distribution
sections.content:
The authors sent a steady flow of letters from locations around Australia, and occasionally from outside it when they travelled abroad. This map view shows the different locations around Sydney from which some of the authors sent letters at different points in time. Mouse over the points to see the names of authors, and zoom out for a wider view.

"Your letter has been travelling round with me in the hope, so far quite vain, that I would find a chance to answer it. It has been nice company anyway—I'll hope to see you next time you are in Sydney, to talk shop & what not. Talking is the greatest sport on earth, though I don't claim to be much good at it." (Marjorie Barnard to Eleanor Dark, 30 Sept 1941)

"Is there any hope of your being in town on Tuesday 14th inst? That night we are discussing Furphy on our members' night. These evenings are for writers per se, and we can go into things more than at the public Sunday lectures ... Louis Esson, Frank Davison, Geo Farwell and KSP [Katharine Susannah Prichard] have promised to come and disagree with me or carry it further. All Furphy lovers urgently needed. Discussion at the FAW [Fellowship of Australian Writers] rooms, 38 Clarence St, 8 pm, Tues Sep. 14" (Miles Franklin to Eleanor Dark, 6 September 1943).

sections.title: Timeline
sections.content: Over the almost three decades that the letters cover, there are burst of activity, and different pairs of correspondents become active at different times. Miles Franklin and Katherine Susannah Prichard's letters, for instance, gradually become fuller and franker through the middle years of the century, and the mutual support their correspondence provides is palpable. "At last a moment with you! I always feel I've got to have time to think to you, as if we were really in communication. Your letters are always so much part of yourself—almost as refreshing as a talk with you" (Prichard to Franklin, 5 November 1952).

sections.title: Visualising correspondence as a network
sections.content:
Visualising the letters as a network enables us to quickly get an overall sense of which writers corresponded the most frequently with each other. The letters make clear their importance as a way for the authors to not only keep in touch with each other, but also to share and discuss developments in the wider field of literary activity both inside and beyond Australia. 

"Frank [Ryland] writes, but his letters become increasingly uninteresting, though I would not like him to think so. But he sends me Voice and an occasional Meanjin, for which I am grateful. Sort of keeps me au fait with down there." (Jean Devanny to Miles Franklin, 27 May 1954)

Some pairs of correspondents, such as Miles Franklin and Katherine Susannah Prichard, lived at opposite ends of the continent and met infrequently, so sustained their friendship with large numbers of letters. However, others, such as Marjorie Barnard and Flora Eldershaw, collaborated in person (publishing under the collective pseudonyn 'Barnard Eldershaw'), so did not need to write to each other so frequently.

sections.title: Intensity of correspondence
sections.content:
This graph plots the date letters were written against the number of words in each letter (a rough proxy for the intensity of the correspondence).

As important as correspondence was, it could also be a burden. "I am having a Sunday answering letters, which have piled up on me. A little while ago I cut down my correspondents, but somehow they have built up again. One drops one, but another takes her place. I have had several letters to answer to England, people who have read my last book and want to come out here on the strength of it. That is about twenty I have had now. I hope no more." (Jean Devanny to Miles Franklin on 24 January 1954)

"I must pluck myself together and pull up my socks and make the effort or whatever the right phrase to answer your letters at last. So many interruptions, so many futile chores, so very little strength, defeats me entirely. This letter was to have gone to you a fortnight ago but that's how it is with me." (Miles Franklin to Katharine Susannah Prichard, 23 Oct 1952)

sections.title: Support, advice and critique
sections.content:
Amongst other things, the authors also helped each other with publishing advice. "You have asked for my advice and I will give it", wrote Miles Franklin to Jean Devanny on 31 October 1953. "I should not send the MS to Harrap at present. If you want another publisher's opinion before you go farther, I could put you in touch with the Melb[ourne] man who did Rex Ingamells' big novel that was rejected by A[ngus] & R[obertson]. But I should not send it there yet either, unless you feel you want to desperately. If it were my own case, this is what I'd do."

While the tone of the letters is generally constructive and supportive, the authors are also capable of giving robust critiques of each others' work. Marjorie Barnard, writing to Eleanor Dark about Dark's recently published novel The Little Company, described how she read the novel "with a sort of perturbation. There are things that it is now axiomatic to say to you—that the book is well architected, has a fine surface, is deftly written. It has all those things. You've partially (but not quite) escaped the formula that seemed to be closing on you —there is still, diluted, the 'accident' as solvent & the rather too overt use of bricklike squares cut-out of the stream of consciousness. You've something to say, & the means developed & matured, of saying it and yet I feel that the book as a whole remains unconsummated. Virgin. As if Ideas & feelings had been set side by side but had never fused" (25 August 1945).
